articles.title_orig: Cornell faculty senate introduces no-confidence resolution over handling of alleged 2024 sexual assault
articles.title_zh: Cornell faculty senate introduces no-confidence resolution over handling of alleged 2024 sexual assault
articles.content_orig:
ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University faculty introduced a resolution declaring a no-confidence vote in the university administration’s handling of the alleged 2024 sexual assault at a fraternity house.
The resolution was submitted to the University Faculty Committee on Monday evening, according to a copy obtained by NBC News.
“That the Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University,” the resolution, which is less than half a page, says.
The measure is expected to be considered by the faculty senate, which meets Oct. 14, according to a statement from faculty senator Paul Ortiz.
“The goal is to really force systemic change,” Ortiz, a professor of labor history, said in a statement.
Ortiz added that “students have been telling us stories they don’t feel safe, and this has been going on for a number of years” and called the situation a “systemic problem.” He reiterated that the senate was not “targeting any individual” but that the students and faculty “have been unsatisfied with the response.”
“Women need to feel safe,” he said.
In a statement accompanying the resolution, the faculty sponsors said “numerous Cornell colleagues” had approached them demanding action, while students had told faculty they were “upset, fearful for their personal safety,” and wanted the Ivy League school to address sexual assault on campus.
Cornell alumni had also contacted faculty members and shared “their own traumatic stories as students,” the statement added.
Cornell declined to comment.
The proposed no-confidence resolution marks an escalation in pressure on Cornell and its administration following national scrutiny over how the case was handled. Last month, a former student identified as Jane Doe sued the university and seven current and former students in connection with the alleged sexual assault.
She alleges that in October 2024 she was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members while she was impaired by alcohol, ketamine and marijuana.
The woman’s allegations have made national headlines for days and prompted protests on the university’s campus after widespread criticism that the university and local officials did not do enough to investigate the woman’s allegations.
Anne Marie Elizabeth Brady, a Faculty Senate member and research director for the university’s Industrial and Labor Relations Workers Institute, said the resolution came together “quickly” in recent days.
“If I was a woman on Cornell’s campus, I’d run in the other direction,” she said. “Because I’m not sure Cornell is there to protect the students the way they should be.”
Brady said that Cornell’s decision to discipline the seven men accused of wrongdoing instead of passing on the case to outside law enforcement “feels like a cover-up to me.”
“If I’m a betting woman, I suspect they didn’t do that because they wanted to keep it secret,” she said. “They wanted to manage the story.”
If the Faculty Senate passes the resolution, Brady said, it will then prompt a series of discussions between faculty and Cornell’s leadership for policies affecting sexual assault.
Similar action was taken last year following years of campus protests of the war in Gaza. Brady says those recommendations have largely been ignored.
“If the administration came out and said: ‘you know what? we screwed up, we did A, B, and C wrong. We failed this student, we failed all our students through this process and these are the concrete ways and steps we are going to take to change,’” she said. “If they did that? That goes so far.”
Adam Reiss and Maggie Vespa reported from Ithaca; Matt Lavietes reported from New York City.
Adam Reiss is a reporter and producer for NBC and MSNBC.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

articles.title_orig: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
articles.title_zh: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
articles.content_orig:
Gov. Gavin Newsom called the president’s remarks "deranged and dangerous."
President Donald Trump suggested that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego if it were allowed to develop a nuclear weapon, drawing condemnation from California leaders, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who called the remarks "deranged and dangerous."
Trump’s comments during a political rally in Nebraska on Monday come in the wake of two foiled terror plots in recent weeks, including an attack on an Israel-bound passenger flight in the Middle East and a potential attack on a U.K. airbase used by the U.S. Air Force. On Monday, prior to the rally, Trump said an Iran-linked threat to the base prompted the U.S. to move its bombers elsewhere.
The investigations into both incidents remain underway, but politicians have drawn tentative links to Tehran. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran played a role in alleged plot that would have targeted the base. Trump said he "personally" believes Iran was behind the attempt to hijack the flight. Neither Burnham nor Trump offered further details to support their statements.
In his speech on Monday, Trump sought to assuage concerns about the economic impact of the Iran war, calling it a "small price to pay for keeping the world safe" and "keeping our country safe."
Defending his war effort, Trump suggested that if Iran was to develop a nuclear weapon, they could "take out" an American city. He then went a step further, singling out two Democratic-led cities in California.
"Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego." The crowd cheered at the remarks.
Los Angeles is the second-most populous city in the United States, while San Diego is home to several major American military installations, including the Naval Base San Diego -- principal homeport of the U.S. Pacific Fleet.
Trump then pivoted back to his messaging on the war, assuring the crowd that the conflict was a "small price to pay" in the grand scheme of things and that the war was "essentially almost over with." "And they might keep going a little long. You know, they always say they have a big threshold for pain. They need it, let me tell you they need it. But it's going to end very soon, and it'll end one way or the other," he added.
The remarks drew swift condemnation from state leaders, including Newsom and the cities’ mayors, and at least one Republican running for Congress in a battleground district.
Jim Desmond, a Republican running for an open congressional seat representing parts of San Diego County, condemned the remarks on social media.
"I vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments. America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland," Desmond, a Navy veteran, wrote. "No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage."
Newsom, who has often sparred with the president, repeatedly condemned Trump’s remarks Monday night, calling them "disgusting and disqualifying" in a second social media post. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass called Trump's remarks "dangerous" and suggested they could "potentially compromise our safety."
"The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives," Bass said in a statement on social media. "In the face of irresponsible threats, as Angelenos, we know how to stand together and protect our city.”
San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria similarly denounced Trump, saying that his city "is not collateral damage."
"We are not expendable," Gloria wrote, telling Trump to "keep our city out of your reckless war talk."
Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, addressed the criticism on Tuesday, saying, "The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality. He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money."

articles.title_orig: Francis Halzen wins Nobel Physics Prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.title_zh: Francis Halzen wins Nobel Physics Prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.content_orig:
Belgian physicist Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for creating a giant detector in Antarctica that captures neutrinos, the so-called “ghost particles” from space that scientists believe offer clues to how the universe evolved.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the prestigious award in Stockholm on Tuesday, crediting Halzen with a central role in building the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.
The neutrino interactions collected by the observatory provide information about how high-energy neutrinos are created and may even reveal previously unknown phenomena, the Academy said.
“It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn’t expect it,” Halzen said, speaking to the committee by phone from Italy, in a call broadcast at the news conference to announce the winner.
The 82-year-old said it was predicted before that he would win the Nobel Prize, but the announcement still made him feel “strange”.
“I am working on a proposal, and I hope that this prize will help getting it approved,” he said to chuckles from the audience.
Neutrinos have nearly no mass and carry no electric charge, so they can cross between planets, stars and human bodies without being altered, making them rare and hard to catch. There are roughly 100 trillion solar and cosmic neutrinos that pass through our bodies every second.
Halzen first proposed the IceCube project in 1988, realising that the clear ice beneath the South Pole could act as a detector, so on the rare occurrence a neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus, it gives off a flash of light that buried sensors can record.
Richard Fitzgerald, editor-in-chief of Physics Today, said although hundreds of people built the observatory, it “all started with one person”, noting that the physics prize has rarely gone to one sole winner in recent years.
“People joined him in the quest for these neutrino messengers. The messenger is bringing information from cosmos,” committee member Eva Olsson said during the news conference. “They opened the door to distant galaxies and tell us about the processes of exploding stars.”
Eva Lindroth, a researcher in Stockholm and a member of the Nobel Committee, told Al Jazeera that Halzen’s observatory has helped scientists understand high-energy particles.
“The nice thing with neutrinos is that they come straight at us,” she said. “That way we can ultimately understand these sources of high-energy particles and understand more about how things in the universe, like how galaxies are formed and the roles of the black holes in that process.
“It gives a new way to study the universe,” Lindroth added. “They give us information which we cannot get in any other way.”
Last year’s award went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for experiments on quantum physics.
On Monday, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to two American scientists for discoveries that helped explain how the brain works.
The next award will be the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, which will be announced on Wednesday in Stockholm.
Nobel laureates will receive their awards in a ceremony on December 10, marking the anniversary of Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel, who established the award; members of the royal families of Sweden and Norway will be in attendance.

articles.title_orig: Corn for feed use seeing dip in China
articles.title_zh: Corn for feed use seeing dip in China
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING, CHINA — China’s grain feed and residual use is forecast to remain broadly stable in 2026-27 as a smaller breeding sow herd limits hog feed demand, partly offset by growth in poultry, aquaculture and ruminant feed, according to a report from the Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) of the US Department of Agriculture.
In its Oct. 1 update, the FAS said 2026-27 corn production is forecast at 306 million tonnes, up from 301.2 million tonnes, with imports projected to recover to 6 million tonnes from a reduced 2025-26 estimate of 4 million tonnes. Corn consumption was lowered 1 million tonnes from the June forecast to 322 million tonnes due to a lower-than-expected percentage of corn in feed and less-than-expected imports.
“The ratio of corn in feed rations is trending lower from 47% in January to 29% in August,” the FAS said. “Hog farming remains deeply unprofitable, accelerating sow herd liquidation. Feed demand is also being squeezed by corn substitutes. Deep farming losses are encouraging producers to use more competitively priced wheat, barley and sorghum instead of corn, further reducing corn’s share in feed rations.”
While China’s 2026-27 wheat production forecast remains unchanged at 141 million tonnes, total consumption is seen reaching 150 million tonnes, up 2 million tonnes from the September outlook due to higher feed use but on par with recent marketing years.
“China’s 2026 wheat market is characterized by sufficient supply, weak flour demand, and strong but potentially temporary feed substitution demand,” the FAS said. “Growth in flour consumption has slowed, while excess milling capacity and weak margins have reduced mill operating rates, limiting demand for high-quality wheat.”
Rough rice production for 2026-27 is forecast to increase slightly to 210 million tonnes due to stable area and higher yields than last year. China’s 2026 early rice production remained steady despite the impact of heavy rainfall and typhoons, the FAS said.
Total rice consumption is projected to be 147.3 million tonnes, down slightly year on year. Broken rice also has become a significant feed market substitute.

articles.title_orig: High-energy neutrino detection captures Nobel prize in physics
articles.title_zh: High-energy neutrino detection captures Nobel prize in physics
articles.content_orig:
By Jamie Durrani 2026-10-06T13:33:00+01:00
Source: © Nobel Prize Outreach/Niklas Elmehed
Francis Halzen is the first solo winner of the physics prize for more than 30 years
The 2026 Nobel prize in physics has been awarded to Belgian astrophysicist Francis Halzen for his work on the detection of high-energy cosmic neutrinos that launched a new era of astronomy. Halzen spearheaded the development of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, which has enabled scientists to track high-energy neutrinos that have reached Earth from the farthest reaches of the universe. It is the first time that the physics prize has been awarded to an individual recipient since 1992, when Georges Charpak was recognised for his work on particle detectors .
Neutrinos are elementary particles released by many different sources, including radioactive substances, the sun and other celestial bodies. But the neutrinos released by highly energetic processes like giant supernovae in the distant universe can have energies far higher than other cosmic neutrinos. As a result, these high-energy neutrinos – which have no charge and almost no mass – travel across the universe barely interacting with other matter and without changing direction or losing energy. This means that when these neutrinos reach the Earth they carry information about extreme environments in distant regions of space that cannot be gathered by monitoring other types of radiation such as light or gamma rays.
But the very properties that make high-energy cosmic neutrinos such useful carriers of information also make them incredibly difficult to detect. In the 1980s, Halzen came up with the idea of building a giant facility at the South Pole, where flashes of blue light given off as neutrinos pass through the Antarctic ice could be tracked. Halzen and his colleague John Learned presented the concept at a conference in Poland in June 1988.
Source: © Johan Jamestad/The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences
The IceCube neutrino observatory is a huge cubic kilometre of ice dotted with sensors that was the brainchild of Halzen
Since then, Halzen, who works at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the US, has spent years developing techniques to detect neutrinos, contributing to projects in Greenland and Antarctica that honed the technology. Eventually, he led an initiative that culminated in the construction of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, in which more than 5000 special sensors are spread across a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice deep below the surface.
The IceCube facility was completed in 2011, and uncovered the first evidence of high-energy cosmic neutrinos just two years later. The project involves more than 450 researchers from 14 countries and has paved the way for further international collaboration to detect cosmic neutrinos. Speaking at the prize announcement, the Nobel committee chair Mark Pearce noted that a global network of neutrino telescopes, based in ice and the oceans, is currently being established, which will allow researchers to ‘monitor all of the sky, all of the time’.
Speaking on the phone immediately after the announcement, Halzen described the award as ‘a great surprise’ and emphasised the critical contributions from his collaborators over the years. ‘When we started this project, everybody realised this was a good idea, but very few thought it would work – including myself,’ he said. ‘So this was an adventure where success was not guaranteed and we were lucky to overcome the various challenges, partly because the talent of collaborators and partly because of luck. It was a long journey, but it finally worked.’

articles.title_orig: US justice department moves to strip citizenship of 40 naturalized citizens
articles.title_zh: US justice department moves to strip citizenship of 40 naturalized citizens
articles.content_orig:
Officials file ‘denaturalization actions’ against people accused of crimes in what they call ‘largest’ such initiative
Donald Trump ’s justice department has moved to strip the citizenship of 40 naturalized citizens accused of crimes in what authorities describe as “the largest” such initiative over a single period during his administration.
US justice department officials on Monday announced the filing of “denaturalization actions” against more than three dozen people alleged to have committed such offenses as “acting as an agent for a foreign government, committing voluntary manslaughter, and aggravated sodomy against a special‑needs man”.
The denaturalization requests in question were submitted in multiple federal courts between 21 August and 2 October, according to the justice department.
The federal Immigration and Nationality Act allows for naturalized US citizenship to be revoked by a federal court if the government proves that it was illegally obtained through concealment of a material fact or willful misrepresentation.
A statement attributed to the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, maintained those at the center of Monday’s announcement “concealed critical facts from the US government and represent serious criminal offenders”.
Trump in previous months had reportedly pushed the US justice department to pursue denaturalization cases en masse. The New York Times reported in April that the justice department had identified at least 384 foreign-born US citizens whose naturalization it wanted to revoke.
Denaturalization requests to courts often involve individuals who lied to government authorities during the naturalization process or obtained citizenship through false marriages. There are also some instances where people who committed criminal offenses can lose their citizenship.
In 2025, the first year of Trump’s second presidency, the justice department filed a memo instructing its civil division to ramp up denaturalization efforts, including by adopting more categories of individuals qualifying for denaturalization – which experts have said has supported the president’s mass deportation agenda .
Because denaturalization cases are costly and require extensive manpower, the justice department has historically pursued them only sporadically.
From 2017 to late 2025, the US denaturalized about 120 people, the Times reported. A justice department official said the initiative reported by the Times in April marked only “the first wave” of citizenship-stripping cases.
after newsletter promotion
“Under President Trump’s leadership, the Department of Justice will continue to employ the denaturalization process to maintain our national security and protect the American people,” Blanche’s statement on Monday said.
The 40 people subject to denaturalization proceedings announced on Monday came from various countries, among them Mexico, China, Iran, Pakistan, and the Philippines.
One of those individuals was Jinchao Wei , a former Chinese-born US navy sailor who was convicted in August 2025 of charges including espionage and unlawfully exporting technical data related to defense articles. Prosecutors have said Wei began plotting to sell military secrets to China months before becoming a US citizen in May 2022 and concealed that conduct during the naturalization process.
Wei was sentenced to more than 16 years in prison.

articles.title_orig: The China Drug Dependency
articles.title_zh: The China Drug Dependency
articles.content_orig:
Council on Foreign Relations
In the spring of 2025, eleven EU health ministers described Europe’s dependence on Chinese medicines as the weak point in Europe’s defense. The warning was accurate but largely ignored. For twenty of fifty-six active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) that German regulators classify as essential to supply, enough of the world’s production sits in China that a disruption there would leave European patients without ready alternatives [PDF].
The more troubling dependency lies one layer down. An ingredient made in India or Europe is still made from something, and those chemical building blocks are more heavily concentrated in China than the ingredients themselves. For metformin, a widely prescribed diabetes drug, roughly one-third of supply is exposed to a disruption in China at the ingredient stage. Count the building block that ingredient is made from, and the figure surpasses four-fifths. The antibiotics amoxicillin and cefpodoxime follow the same pattern. Europe can buy its ingredients from non-Chinese manufacturers and remain dependent on China all the same.
Europe inflicted this damage on itself. These dependencies are the result of decades of cost containment in European health systems, which squeezed margins on generic drugs until production left the continent. China, in turn, undertook an equally deliberate industrial policy to build the capacity Europe had shed.
In April 2026, Washington put additional pressure on the EU by announcing tariffs of up to 100 percent on imports of patented medicines and their ingredients, with European products capped at 15 percent. Generic drugs are exempt for now but will be subject to a review due within a year. Europe therefore faces a strategic question with a short fuse: whether to build resilience alone or with partners—and if with partners, on what terms. Partnership is the stronger choice, but on terms that leave Europe’s own pricing, procurement, and regulatory decisions untouched.
Three features of the drug dependency problem make a transatlantic answer more compelling than a purely European one. First, the exposure is shared, and it sits upstream. The U.S. Commerce Department’s investigation found that only around 15 percent of patented APIs by volume are made in the United States. On antibiotics, the concentration is even starker: China supplied roughly 70 percent [PDF] of U.S. antibiotic ingredient imports by volume in 2024, reversing the position of European producers, who held three-quarters of that market in the early 1990s. Neither Europe nor the United States is dealing with a national vulnerability. They are dealing with the same chokepoint, at the same layer of the value chain, in the same molecules.
Second, Europe holds assets that other regions do not. The last large-scale, fully integrated penicillin production site in the Western world is in Austria; the United States has no domestic capacity for making penicillin ingredients or their core precursor. In biologics, or medications that come from living organisms, Europe, along with North America, dominates not only the manufacture of biological ingredients but also the wider production system behind them: the engineered cell lines that produce the drug molecule, the nutrient mixtures those cells grow in, and the chemical solutions that keep the product stable while it is purified. Chinese and Indian producers are still catching up in that segment. Europe can therefore approach Washington as a supplier or co-supplier of security, not a supplicant for it.
Third, unilateral onshoring on both sides is self-defeating, and the current U.S. measures are counterproductive. Europe is the only ally with the penicillin capacity Washington lacks. Tariffs on European medicines raise costs across that base. Extending the regime to generic drugs, which the pending review could do, would reach the most fragile part of European production, where every plant closure is a market share transfer to China. The political effect is worse than the commercial one. Each coercive measure against Europe drains support in European capitals for the transatlantic option and strengthens the argument that resilience should mean autonomy from everyone. If the United States’ objective is an allied answer to Chinese dominance, current instruments are producing the opposite result.
The terms of cooperation matter from Europe’s perspective as well. A strategy that trades one dependency for another is not resilience. Several instruments now on the table in Washington would do exactly that: tariff relief conditioned on relocating production to the United States, drug-pricing commitments negotiated company by company under tariff pressure, and procurement rules with extraterritorial reach [PDF] that determine which suppliers European firms may use. Europe should cooperate on capacity, information, and standards, while retaining sovereign control over pricing, procurement, and regulatory decisions. Any proposal must meet a simple test: if the partnership broke down, Europe must still be able to supply its patients.
Europe and the United States should begin where cooperation costs nothing politically. They could start by fixing their lack of visibility into their own upstream flows of key starting materials. Joint mapping, which builds on the work of the Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority and its U.S. counterparts, is a technical exercise that produces shared information and nothing else. It changes no tariff, no procurement rule, and no market access, so neither side has to concede anything to take part. They should also undertake joint stress-testing on a shared methodology that measures not just how much production sits in China but how long replacement would take if production stopped. In particular, NATO should incorporate the defense-relevant subset of the stress-testing—demand for antibiotics, analgesics, and anesthetics under mobilization conditions—into its resilience work.
Europe should also lock in the existing carve-out under the 2025 United States-European Union Framework —which already grants near-zero treatment to generic medicines, their ingredients, and chemical precursors—and press to make it permanent, including for biosimilars, the lower-cost follow-on versions of biologic drugs whose patents have expired, before the U.S. review of generics concludes.
Europe should legislate its own rules on sensitive biotech and health-data cooperation with China rather than importing American ones through contractual reach. But the U.S. approach warrants careful study. In principle, a plurilateral critical-medicines arrangement modeled on the allied approach now emerging for critical raw materials would make sense. That would include giving preferential treatment to ally-produced ingredients and precursors, mutually recognizing the validity of the other side’s inspections, and establishing common resilience criteria in public procurement. The United States and Europe should establish such a framework with India, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom, among others. The idea would be to coordinate demand: agreeing to long-term purchase commitments that give investors enough certainty to finance new Western production. The binding constraint on that capacity is not technology but price, with European ingredients running up to 40 percent more than Chinese ones. Only guaranteed demand closes that gap. Currently, however, transatlantic relations lack the trust required for such a comprehensive plurilateral arrangement.
The United States’ and Europe’s dependency on Chinese pharmaceutical ingredients was built over decades, and it will not be undone quickly. Europe should start with what can be done now: mapping the upstream flows neither side can currently see, testing how long replacement would actually take, and locking in the generics carve-out before the review closes it. None of that requires trust that does not exist

Flags were lowered in honor of an Army airman from Kentucky who died during World War II, but was not accounted for until November 2025.
U.S. Army Air Forces Private First Class Weber S. Underwood, 25, of Hopkinsville, Kentucky, was a member of the 28th Materiel Squadron, 20th Air Base Group, when Japanese forces invaded the Philippine Islands in December of 1941.

articles.title_orig: China Is Winning the AI Race Trump Won’t Run
articles.title_zh: China Is Winning the AI Race Trump Won’t Run
articles.content_orig:
It matters who writes the rules of the road as artificial intelligence is deployed in every industry in our lives, but the rulebook of policies, regulations and ethical guidelines could look very different depending on who writes it. China and the United States should be fighting for the pen, but America is barely in the running.
China wants to work with the U.S. to jointly govern AI , according to its leader, Xi Jinping , who said in his recent state visit to Washington, D.C., that both nations had a responsibility to “manage AI for good.” “Good” for Beijing means AI models not only must remain under human control but also under the oversight of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
This summer, China created the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, or WAICO. This global AI governing body was designed to capture small and middle-income powers that find themselves outside the U.S. tech boom for political and ideological reasons and for their lack of relevant industry and resources. Beijing is offering these countries a say in AI rule-making because it knows the technology will only be as powerful as the framework that controls it.
In America, the world’s leading AI labs are shouting the loudest for regulation. President Donald Trump sees an irony in that and believes whoever makes the best AI will get to make the rules too. He’s half right: the global AI rule-maker will need buy-in from its users too—and China is already halfway there.
Technology has always outpaced regulation; it was the case with the internet and it will be the same with AI. The world may not be asking enough questions about who should govern AI and how, but the potential answers are already beginning to fragment along geopolitical lines.
Since 2018, China has hosted the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai with the aim of institutionalizing its role in governing the technology now and in the future. Many of WAICO's 37 members are on America’s AI cooperation blacklist: Cuba, Iran and Russia are unlikely to meet U.S. trust standards for technology sharing, ever. But if the United Nations has taught China anything, it’s the utility of securing votes from the forgotten corners of the world to legitimize its positions and demonstrate the hypocrisy of U.S. values.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres attended WAICO’s inauguration and praised China for including the Global South. Technology “cannot be governed by a handful of countries or a handful of companies,” he said.
Observers say China moved to formalize WAICO after the U.S. established Pax Silica in December, 2025. The coalition of West-aligned countries seeks secure, end-to-end supply chains for the full AI tech stack , from data centers and power grids to critical minerals and advanced computer chips.
Aside from mineral-rich Kazakhstan, whose resources make it valuable to both rival AI blocs, Pax Silica’s 24 signatories are mostly high-income economies whose accelerated AI industries are threatening to leave the rest behind. The group’s economic security mandate is to reinforce the U.S.’ systemic advantages over China , but it lacks a voice on AI governance or safety.
The U.S. appears dismissive of WAICO, which for now is without concrete commitments beyond the principle of governance. But that won’t worry Beijing as long as Washington offers no viable alternative. It means the China-led body could become the first multinational institution to set agendas and draft treaties in the name of good AI without America’s input.
Beijing is offering its friends something arguably more valuable than a seat at the table: the technology itself. Outside of China, WAICO’s members have little to no AI industry and therefore are the perfect candidates to adopt the Chinese AI stack. Beijing is only too happy to spread its tech through existing channels like the Belt and Road Initiative infrastructure export program.
“If Chinese firms become major providers of AI models and their corresponding cloud services, data centers, and energy grids, then China may also gain influence over technical standards, data practices, content controls, and what defines responsible AI in the first place,” emerging technologies consultant Hugh Harsono wrote in The Diplomat on Tuesday.
China could dilute U.S. leadership in AI through pure scale by ensuring Chinese labs have more customers than their American competitors, and by encouraging friendly governments to adopt its rules.
China would love for America to join WAICO and bolster its credentials as AI governor, but it benefits from the opposite too: Beijing is poised to tell the world that it tried and failed to convince the U.S. to help make AI safer together.
Beijing has spent years preparing for this moment. In the last six months, the Chinese government has issued guidelines for the development of AI agents, made rules on the behavior of human-like AI services and announced plans to regulate data used in embodied AI—software carried inside physical bodies like humanoid robots or drones .
China was always going to be a first mover on regulation because it has deep concerns about AI’s ability to empower the public to create and share unsanctioned information online, directly or indirectly fueling narratives that could undermine the CCP’s authority.
Like in Iran, Chinese embassies and state media outlets have used AI in their social media-driven propaganda campaigns against the West, but they’re much more conservative back home. Xi doesn’t have a social media account, but even if he did, he wouldn’t be posting the type of generative AI content that Trump has popularized on Truth Social.
The U.S. president has fully embraced the technology for its creative and economic potential and is convinced the AI industry will benefit from a small government approach. He warned Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and others that the AI industry would collapse under the weight of regulation —and that China would win.
In China, where mass communication and strict online censorship by the state have coexisted for three decades, its leaders don’t have the luxury of waiting around to see what AI could do next.
Chen Yixin, who as minister of state security is China’s top spy, said in an essay last month that the CCP’s answer to Western concerns about rogue AI agents was to ensure total Party authority over the technology in order to safeguard the core values of state power, information control and social stability, in the pursuit of regime security.
Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis wants the U.S. to lead a global AI standards group, Sam Altman of OpenAI wants the technology to be governed by a members-led organization like the International Atomic Energy Agency, and Anthropic’s Amodei wants AI models to be scrutinized by a technical body like the Federal Aviation Administration.
China now has the answer to all three, and the rules it makes at home are ready for export.
“The United States cannot credibly propose international standards for regulating frontier AI while at the same time lacking a coherent national set of regulations,” tech analysts Chris Collins and Aalok Mehta said in a report last month for the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“China has realized this and is therefore making a dedicated AI law. Therefore, developing a federal framework to regulate AI would give U.S. diplomacy a model to offer other countries,” they said.
A version of this article was published in Newsweek's China Decoded newsletter on Saturday, October 3. Sign up here .

A new Radio World ebook considers trends in consoles and control surfaces. In this companion piece, Mark Ruddy takes our questions. He’s chief engineer at WVIA Public Media , covering Northeast and Central Pennsylvania.
Radio World: Mark, what do you consider the most important trend in the design of consoles and control surfaces for radio broadcast studios?
Mark Ruddy: It seems that consoles are trending as less of a hardware item, and more of a software item.
The shift to an on-screen console seems that it can work for some applications, but I am happy to see that innovations continue in hardware-based control surfaces. Being a radio station that operates with live personnel, they are familiar with the layout of a hardware-based console. The most important functions for me as an engineer are to see levels for a source that is loaded into a channel and for the surface to function reliably and accurately.
Even though control surfaces are trending smaller, it is good that options still remain for larger layouts and designs.
RW: What is the definition of a radio console now?
Ruddy: In most cases, it is akin to a keyboard for a computer. It is there and functions as a radio console, but really with other means to connect, it is less critical of a component for operation. The exception does exist still for analog or digital-based consoles, but when audio isn’t passing directly though the console, it’s more of an interface.
RW: How has their evolution changed the way engineers view them and plan around their installation?
Ruddy: The evolution of consoles into control surfaces has certainly made things more efficient and effective when planning installation. In most cases it is just running a network cable and power, with the audio entering the system through other means, the installation of a control surface is much neater and in the case of AoIP, it keeps wiring localized and minimizes cable runs.
RW: To what extent has scripting changed console operations, and what does scripting make possible?
Ruddy: Scripting allows for more under-the-hood tasks to be accomplished without anybody realizing what it is doing. Even by doing simple routes or logic controls, it’s very much more efficient.
If you have an automation system that integrates with your installation, it makes things even easier for an operator by being able to execute a hotkey and not having to worry about anything else.
RW: How vibrant is the marketplace for analog consoles?
Ruddy: I believe that there is still a need for analog consoles and will be. Some stations don’t need much more than that for their operations, and they are very useful for at-home studios. Current analog consoles make for a cost-effective upgrade for an aging console.
RW: Any suggested best practices or common errors to avoid when choosing one?
Ruddy: Just recognize your requirements, then make sure to research all available options. What is right for one operation isn’t necessarily right for another. There are many manufacturers making quality consoles and systems, but each one does have its pros and cons. I would also say to reach out to other stations or groups who are using the system you’re looking at to get their opinion and run questions by them as well. That was invaluable for me in choosing our current system.

By Charity L. Cohen / 10/06/2026 Alumni , College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences
EAST GREENSBORO, N.C. (Oct. 6, 2026) – Forever a North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University Aggie and now a Hillman College Falcon, former Mister A&T Joshua Suiter ‘22 is starring in the Netflix reboot of the 1980s and 1990s hit sitcom “A Different World.”
The series, which debuted at No. 1 on Netflix in the U.S., has already been renewed for a second season. It builds on the cultural impact of the original series, which helped shape national perceptions of historically Black college and university (HBCU) life and inspired generations of students.
Following a new generation of students at the iconic fictional HBCU, Hillman College, the sequel explores the lives of today’s students while examining the legacy of those who came before them. The series’ writing team includes Ashley Laverne Jackson, daughter of late civil rights leader the Rev. Jesse Jackson ‘64.
Suiter portrays Andre, a fellow student and classmate of Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), daughter of original characters Whitley (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison). As Deborah begins her journey at Hillman, she works to establish her own identity beyond her parents’ legacy while experiencing the highs and challenges of campus life.
“Seeing all the love for Andre really hit home,” Suiter said. “He’s one of my favorite characters thus far, and we created him from scratch, so to know that the hard work is being received and folks want more encourages me to keep going.”
Suiter discovered his calling for acting and musical theater at 7, quickly realizing that hours spent studying lines and practicing techniques felt like minutes. That passion led him to N.C. A&T, where he earned a B.A. in professional theatre from the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences.
While at A&T, Suiter built a strong foundation in the performing arts, gaining experience both on stage and behind the scenes. One of his notable performances was in “Ain’t Misbehavin’” during the university’s first Town & Gown Gala in 2019, where he first met Guy, who reprises her role as Whitley in the reboot.
In addition to acting, Suiter worked as a theater technician and developed skills in the marketing and business aspects of performance and the entertainment industry. This versatility helped propel him into his professional career.
“I came in as a creative, but what A&T did between Alpha Phi Alpha, the classes, talking business with professors and serving as Mister A&T sharpened me on the business side,” said Suiter. “It sharpened my networking skills while showing me how to be authentic to who I am.”
As a talented and emerging actor who most recently appeared in the Hulu series “All’s Fair,” performing alongside prominent Hollywood actors, starring in “A Different World” represents a full-circle moment for Suiter as an HBCU alumnus, bringing him into a reimagined version of a series he grew up watching.
“When you talk about an HBCU experience, I’m putting mine up there with the best of them,” he said. “I have so many experiences to pull from with the run of this show, with the character Andre. Hillman even has a heartbeat of its own, so it’s been fun exploring what that feels like as a student there, while still carrying that Aggie Pride in my heart.”

articles.title_zh: Hidden Beauty: UVM student explores Lake Champlain’s underwater world
articles.content_orig:
A University of Vermont Ph.D. student is sharing the hidden beauty of Lake Champlain’s underwater ecosystem with thousands of social media followers, blending research and creativity.
A University of Vermont Ph.D. student is sharing the hidden beauty of Lake Champlain’s underwater ecosystem with thousands of social media followers, blending research and creativity.
Graham Montague, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Vermont, is diving into Lake Champlain to showcase its underwater wonders and sharing his discoveries with thousands of followers online.
"I started doing just for a creative outlet and just to make videos that I wanted to actually see myself," Montague said. "I do this all the time anyways, but I started taking my GoPro with me and just started filming fish underneath the water just for fun."
Since 2023, Montague has been documenting life beneath the surface, highlighting underwater vegetation, shipwrecks, and various fish species. His passion for aquatic exploration began with a backyard stream at the Cuyahoga Valley National Park in northeastern Ohio.
"There's so much cool things to see underneath water, but if you're not actually in the water, you're not going to be able to see them," Montague said. "To highlight the beauty of the underwater species is super fun. And it also just gets me outside."
Montague’s academic work focuses on natural resources, aquatic ecology, and fisheries. His current research at UVM examines Lake Champlain’s distinct basins, each with unique environments and fish populations, and tracks how stocked Atlantic salmon move between them.
"We've been tracking them for a couple of years now, and we're finding that Atlantic salmon are moving very far distances throughout the lake and even potentially out of the lake, which is super cool," Montague said.
Between his research and social media videos, Montague hopes to inspire others to explore and protect nature, whether in their own backyard or beneath the surface of a lake.
"The backyard stream in your backyard is going to have a lot of cool fish and wildlife too. That also needs to be conserved and protected and love," Montague said. "So just get outside, enjoy nature, and really just follow what you're passionate about."
Montague’s work demonstrates that you don’t have to look far, or stay above the surface to find something worth protecting.

articles.title_orig: Chanel is all about joy as Blazy celebrates year at helm of world’s hottest brand
articles.title_zh: Chanel is all about joy as Blazy celebrates year at helm of world’s hottest brand
articles.content_orig:
Artistic director is all smiles as he swaps quiet luxury for bold colours and patterns at Paris show
“It’s a good start,” Matthieu Blazy said after a Paris show that marked a year of his tenure as artistic director at Chanel . “I am happy with where we are at.”
Chanel now holds the top spot in the Lyst index of the world’s hottest brands, which tracks demand and engagement across search and social media. The privately held company announces official financial results only once a year, but figures reported by Bloomberg showed 16% growth in the first half of 2026. In Vanity Fair’s list of the world’s 50 most powerful people, published this month, Blazy is the only fashion designer to make the cut. People who don’t much care about fashion have noticed him; people who do care about fashion talk about him non-stop.
Blazy’s Chanel is about joy. Smiley and chatty in person, he enthuses about his team and the women he dresses, presenting a friendly face of Chanel that contrasts with Karl Lagerfeld’s legendary acid tongue and Coco’s controlled brutalist chic. He talks about his job like a child in a candy store, not a tortured artist: he got the idea for this stage set, a flock of 95 giant white birds suspended from the domed steel and glass ceiling of the Grand Palais in Paris, while on holiday in southern Italy with his partner, watching migrating birds fly above the Crati River.
One of Chanel’s most famous adverts of the 1990s featured Vanessa Paradis in a birdcage ; now, Chanel’s birds fly free. For the soundtrack of the show Blazy had asked Nicole Kidman to read a passage “about time, about freedom” from Virginia Woolf’s To The Lighthouse, which he had read on that Italian holiday. Fashion was “women’s homemade remedy for the dark times”, he said.
After several years when the decaffeinated aesthetic of quiet luxury dominated fashion, the new Chanel shouts with cereal-aisle colours. A red and white embroidered jacket with a jade and turquoise skirt, plus bag and boots in navy and gold. The iconic two-tone pumps, but in zebra stripes and yellow polka dots instead of the traditional camel and black.
The same model opened and closed the show carrying Gabrielle Chanel’s very own 2.55 handbag. “Gabrielle actually had very few bags in her own life, which is something I find quite beautiful. So this bag is not broken, but it has a wonderful patina,” Blazy said.
after newsletter promotion
On his moodboard were photographs of the founder he had found in the archive: Gabrielle as a child; with Gigot, her beloved great dane; on a boat; riding a horse; in a Harlequin fancy dress costume; smiling in a bold leopard-print coat and matching hat. “It is a side of Chanel that is not known: her funny side, her joyful side. I see women as a juxtaposition of so many selves, and Chanel had this incredible layering within herself.”
The famous soft-shouldered Chanel suit came worn with nothing beneath, “like perfume” (Blazy, a student of Cocology, will not have missed the allusion to what Marilyn Monroe famously said she wore in bed: Chanel No 5). “I like the idea that when you wear it directly on the skin, it makes a fetish of the suit. A little punk Chanel,” he said. A year of fabric innovation was behind the newest versions of the suit, a smocked silk on an elasticated membrane, which “is my answer to what sporty could mean at Chanel”, Blazy said.

The S&P 500 rose to a fresh all-time intraday high on Tuesday, boosted by gains in key technology names as well as declines in oil prices and Treasury yields.
The broad market index was last up 0.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 205 points, or 0.4%. The Nasdaq Composite added 0.5% and had hit a new all-time high as well.
The moves higher were bolstered by a rise in chipmakers. Shares of Marvell Technology popped 7%, while others such as Nvidia and Broadcom traded up around 1% each.
Additionally, the benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield fell 2 basis points to 5.29% after scaling to levels not seen since 2002 on Monday. The 2-year Treasury yield declined 3 basis points to 4.802%.
Bonds have been volatile over the past six weeks, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management investment chief Lisa Shalett said in a note to clients. She cited a potentially new Fed policy framework, economic growth and high oil prices while the Middle East conflict stretches on as factors.
"Nevertheless, while intraday implied volatility has risen, the six-week stretch has not reached the extremes that catalyzed the 2022 equity bear market," Shalett wrote.
Traders are now looking ahead to the Federal Reserve's minutes from its September meeting due Wednesday, which could shed some light on policymakers' move to raise rates.
Alongside Treasury yields, a drop in oil prices also gave equities a boost Tuesday. Brent crude traded 2% lower at around $98 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate futures shed 1% to roughly $87 a barrel.
Bond yields may peak in the next month, Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok wrote Tuesday, citing "several forces" that suggest a top between now and early November, among them the increased odds of some sort of resolution in the Middle East ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the U.S.
Other signals include the move by the U.S. and European allies to release additional oil supplies, putting further downward pressure on crude oil prices, and harm being inflicted on the housing and auto industries by higher interest rates.
Slok said that 84% of global fixed income now yields more than 3%, "up from just 12% in January 2022."  Any deal "or government action that lowers oil prices would ease the upward pressure on interest rates at a time when yields are already elevated across nearly the entire global bond market," he said.
David Rosenberg of Rosenberg Research in Toronto, a former chief North American economist at Merrill Lynch, said bond pressures are easing Tuesday as oil prices fall another 1% and European bond prices rally, noting that earlier in the day benchmark yields on Italian government debt dropped 11 basis points to 4.52%, in France by 10 bps to 4.76% and in the U.K. by 6 bps to 5.36%.
Shares of Marvell Technology jumped more than 7% in morning trading on Tuesday after the company provided long-term revenue guidance at its Investor Day.
Marvell expects its revenue for fiscal 2028 to come in at $20 billion, above the $18.17 billion that analysts polled by FactSet were looking for.
Looking out even further, the company sees its revenue being between $70 billion and $90 billion in fiscal 2031. That's well above the consensus estimate of $47.04 billion.
The latest move in the stock puts its year-to-date surge at more than 242%.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite traded at record levels on Tuesday morning.
The broad market index rose 0.5% shortly after the opening bell, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 189 points, or 0.4%.

articles.title_zh: Mapping where US bombers are based globally
articles.content_orig:
Over the course of Sunday, a dozen B-1B bombers took off from Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford in western England and flew home to the United States. Their departure abruptly ended the base’s role as a launchpad for US strikes on Iran, which began on February 28.
The base, roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, is the US Air Force’s only European airfield for heavy bombers and a key forward operating location for deployed bombers.
Over the past two weeks, six people were arrested on suspicion of “terrorism”. They were all released on bail.
US President Donald Trump said on Monday the bombers were moved because “there were some threats”, which he believed were linked to Iran. “So we moved them around a little bit, not very far,” he told reporters at the White House.
Hours earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down any link to the alleged plot, saying it was “not unusual to see rotations happen” and that he had confidence in the security of US bases.
On September 27, police arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near Fairford in the United Kingdom. They were released on bail a day later.
Investigators found petrol but no explosive devices in their vans, though UK officials say the men remain under investigation . On Thursday, police arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack on the airbase. He was also released on bail on October 3.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot but declined to give details. Iran has denied any such scheme and summoned the UK ambassador in Tehran in protest at the arrests.
The US Air Force flies three types of bombers, with a fourth on the way.
The B-52 Stratofortress is the oldest. The B-52H model currently in service was built in the early 1960s. With a wingspan of 56 metres (185 feet), it is the largest US bomber and can carry about 31 tonnes of weapons, including nuclear bombs and cruise missiles.
The B-1B Lancer , which entered service in the mid-1980s, is the fastest of the three. It can reach 1.2 times the speed of sound and has a swing-wing that sweeps back for high-speed flight. It carries the largest conventional payload, about 34 tonnes, but no longer carries nuclear weapons. These were the aircraft that left Fairford.
The B-2 Spirit is a flying-wing stealth bomber designed to slip past air defences. Only 20 were built, of which 19 remain in service. It can carry both nuclear and conventional weapons, including the 13,600kg (30,000lb) “bunker buster” bomb used in US strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites in June 2025.
The B-21 Raider , a smaller stealth bomber, is still in flight testing, and it remains on track for delivery in 2027. Over the next decade and a half, the air force plans to replace the B-1B and B-2, leaving a future fleet of B-21s and upgraded B-52s.
All US bombers are permanently based in the US, at five main airbases:
All of these bases have long, wide runways, typically exceeding 10,000 feet (3,048 metres).
That makes bomber runways about as long as those at a big international airport. What limits where bombers can operate is not tarmac but security, weapons storage and support.
For missions abroad, the US rotates bombers through a handful of forward bases. Other important overseas operating locations include Andersen Air Force Base in Guam and Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean.
Beyond these, the air force sends small groups of bombers to allied airbases for a few weeks at a time, in what it calls Bomber Task Force deployments. Recent rotations have included B-52s at Moron in Spain, B-1Bs at Orland in Norway and Misawa in Japan, and B-52s at Tindal in northern Australia, which arrived in September.
The bombers can also go on a strike mission from the US with the help of aerial refuelling. Bomber missions during the US-Israel war on Iran lasted more than 30 hours there and back. Each group of three bombers needed six to nine tanker aircraft to refuel them along the way.

Wildfire risk is expanding across regions and seasons, increasing the regulatory, financial and reliability pressures facing electric utilities. Because every system has different environmental conditions, infrastructure and operational requirements, effective mitigation requires more than a single solution. Utilities need a layered strategy that combines wildfire prevention, early detection and response.
Designed for utility standards engineers, wildfire program managers and other professionals responsible for grid resilience, this webinar will examine how utilities can evaluate and combine mitigation approaches across overhead and underground distribution systems. Attendees will explore practical considerations for reducing ignition risk, limiting fault energy and improving the detection and isolation of potentially hazardous faults.
Attendees will learn how to:
• Structure a layered mitigation strategy around prevention, detection and emergency response
• Evaluate grid-hardening approaches, including covered equipment and undergrounding
• Apply protection technologies that reduce fault energy, sparks and debris
• Incorporate high-impedance fault detection, weather monitoring and operational measures
• Consider CAL FIRE-compliant equipment within wildfire mitigation plans and standards
You will leave with a practical framework for assessing available strategies and identifying the combination of engineering, protection and operational measures best aligned with their utility’s risk profile and wildfire mitigation objectives.
Alice Stage is the Utility Marketing Manager at Eaton , where she leads strategic marketing initiatives focused on helping utilities navigate grid modernization, electrification, and resilience challenges. She works closely with utility customers, industry partners, and Eaton subject matter experts to develop programs and events that foster collaboration and innovation across the energy sector.

He brings more than 13 years of experience in electric utilities, power systems, and infrastructure engineering, supporting utilities across Canada in the areas of distribution system reliability, grid modernization, and wildfire mitigation. Yasir has worked extensively with utilities on wildfire prevention and risk mitigation initiatives, providing technical guidance on grid hardening strategies, utility operational practices, and the application of technologies that help reduce ignition risk and improve system resilience. He serves on CSA Technical Subcommittees for Distribution Transformers and Insulation Coordination, participates in the ESA Ontario Capital Equipment Working Group, and is an active member of EFC, USF, CIGRE Canada, and EDA. articles.title_orig: Russia’s neighbor backs push to lift ban on nuclear weapons, prompting outcry from Moscow
articles.title_zh: Russia’s neighbor backs push to lift ban on nuclear weapons, prompting outcry from Moscow
articles.content_orig:
The Kremlin on Tuesday warned a preliminary decision by Lithuanian lawmakers to lift a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons and the potential deployment of a NATO military base in the country will mark "another significant escalation" of regional tensions.
The comments come shortly after Lithuania's parliament voted in favor of advancing a constitutional change on deploying nuclear weapons on its territory. It is the first of two ballots required for the change, with the latter scheduled for Jan. 12 next year.
The country, which is a member of both the European Union and NATO and shares a border with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave on the Baltic Sea, has been looking to remove the constitutional ban to strengthen its resilience amid growing security concerns.
Lithuania has been one of Ukraine's staunchest allies during Russian President Vladimir Putin 's more than 4½-year conflict with Kyiv, providing extensive military equipment and financial support.
President Donald Trump , meanwhile, said he would consider Lithuania's request for a permanent U.S. military base in the country. "They are friends of mine. They are great people, so we will certainly look at it," Trump said Monday.
Asked about the developments, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that they "cannot be perceived as anything other than a step toward escalating tensions, just as the deployment of nuclear weapons in a neighboring country cannot," according to Russian state news agency Tass.
"Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary, they will, to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions. As for Russia, of course, Moscow will be forced to take all necessary measures to guarantee its own security," Peskov said.
Article 137 of Lithuania's constitution explicitly prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction and the establishment of foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory. The proposed amendment, which will require the support of at least 94 of the 141 members of parliament to pass, would remove that provision.
Lithuanian Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said scrapping the restriction would bolster the country's resilience and remove a legal distinction between Lithuania and other EU and NATO countries.
"We will ensure stronger support that could be available to us," Olekas said, according to state broadcaster LRT .
"By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal," he added.

articles.title_orig: World-expanding stories from Pitt’s Nationality and Heritage Rooms
articles.title_zh: World-expanding stories from Pitt’s Nationality and Heritage Rooms
articles.content_orig:
From the latest big breakthrough to the most influential and inspiring figures on campus to Pitt in the community, Pittwire is your official source for what’s happening now.
Kati Csoman was still an undergraduate at the University of Pittsburgh when she lived in Hungary for the first time.
She spent the summer of 1988 in the rural northeastern village where her father had grown up. She slept in cousins’ homes, some of which didn’t have indoor plumbing. She picked up Hungarian with a village accent and, for the first time in her life, the language she heard at her childhood kitchen table became something she could speak back.
The immersion into this experience came courtesy of a Nationality Rooms scholarship .
“It really helped me to connect to that part of my life, which is so deeply a part of me,” she says. Three years later, she arrived back in Budapest on a state department fellowship to the U.S. embassy, watching firsthand how Hungary would remake itself after her father’s country voted in its first free elections since the 1940s.
“But, also, it totally changed my academic trajectory and then changed my professional trajectory, too.”
The scholarship launched Csoman (A&S ’89, SPIA ’96G) on a career in international education and connected her not only to her family’s history but also to a broader appreciation of ethnic communities and cross-cultural experiences.
And, eventually, it would lead her back to where it all began.
Today, Csoman is director of Pitt’s Nationality Rooms and Intercultural Exchange Programs, home to 31 spaces inside the Cathedral of Learning that represent the cultural heritages of many of Pittsburgh’s international communities.
The rooms were first imagined in the mid-1920s by Chancellor John Bowman, who wanted a celebration of Pittsburgh’s multicultural presence at the heart of his planned Cathedral of Learning . He turned to Ruth Crawford Mitchell, a Pitt sociologist already closely associated with the city’s ethnic communities through her work with second-generation immigrant students. She gave the program its shape at a time when nearly half of Pittsburgh residents were either born abroad or the children of immigrants. Communities could sponsor classrooms in the Cathedral and, once room construction was complete, leftover funds supported scholarships to send Pitt students abroad year after year. [Watch: Pitt's Nationality and Heritage Rooms are also celebrating a centennial this year. ]
Mitchell stepped back from the directorship in 1957. Shepherd Witman, who arrived at Pitt the following year to direct the Office of Cultural and Educational Exchange, oversaw the rooms during a transitional period, while E. Maxine Bruhns would take the reins in 1965. Bruhns led the Nationality Rooms for the next 55 years, when 12 of the 31 rooms were dedicated and scholarship programs were expanded significantly. Bruhns retired in 2020, with Csoman succeeding her the following year.
But the rooms touched Csoman’s own family long before. Her maternal grandfather had given a dime to help build the Cathedral. Csoman’s father later served on the Hungarian Room Committee, and Csoman herself volunteered with it before becoming the program’s director.
Since the late 1940s, the Nationality Rooms program has supported more than 1,800 Pitt undergrads or graduate students with study abroad scholarships, awarding nearly $5 million in funding. Thirty committees, plus the Women’s International Club, still meet; they fundraise and produce intercultural programming for the campus and wider community, and nearly all of the rooms presently serve as active classrooms or gathering places.
From conceptualization to fundraising to dedication, Pittsburgh’s international communities have shaped each of the rooms into a cultural self-portrait. Every room is designed with precise choices about what best represents a community and how it wants to be seen. A century in, the following stories, centered on the Chinese (dedicated 1939) , Italian (1949) , African Heritage (1989) and Philippine (2019) rooms, reveal examples of how these spaces bridge past and present and often reshape a life’s trajectory.
The Chinese community was not on Mitchell’s original list. In her earliest report to Bowman, Mitchell named 14 ethnic groups interested in building rooms; most were Eastern, Central or Southern European.
While the Chinese community was kept small in the United States by the Immigration Act of 1924 and other federal policies, a group of Chinese graduate students at Pitt sought out Bowman anyway. The Chancellor told them that if they could fundraise and form a committee, they could have a room, says Michael Walter, current manager of education programs for the Nationality Rooms. They organized quickly.
City-wide development also had a significant impact on Pittsburgh’s Chinese community at that time.
The city’s Chinatown neighborhood spanned multiple blocks downtown, but ended up physically divided in the 1920s and 1930s by construction of the city’s Boulevard of the Allies. Pittsburgh’s Chinatown district was all but gone in the following decades with residents moving outward.
Still, the Chinese Room became one of the first nine rooms at Pitt to reach completion. The German, Russian, Scottish, Swedish and Early American rooms were dedicated in 1938, while the Chinese, Czechoslovak, Hungarian and Yugoslav rooms came next in 1939.
The Chinese Room was modeled on an 18th-century reception hall in Beijing’s Forbidden City, the imperial palace at the heart of Ming and Qing dynasty rule.
This art installation inside Hillman Library examines a century of Nationality Rooms history. The installation will run through July 2027.
Yuefang Chang, a research associate professor in Pitt’s School of Medicine’s Department of Neurological Surgery, has been involved with the room for more than a decade, chairing the Chinese Room Committee for the past year and a half.
Chang has worked to learn the room’s history herself, noting that “even within the Chinese community, if they didn’t get a chance to go to the University, they just don’t know about its existence here.”
The first time Chang walked into the room, it surprised her. She had expected the colors to look brighter; instead, the dragons and phoenixes had softened over the decades.
But age and history are essential parts of the experience. Each Nationality Room’s design draws on cultural and traditional markers from before 1787 — the year of Pitt’s founding — meaning every room depicts something far older than the present. Decades of classes, holiday open houses and committee gatherings have only deepened that. Time is the point.
The Chinese Room is full of imperial signifiers: a five-clawed dragon on the ceiling (only the imperial dragon has five, a marker of leadership), phoenixes among peony blossoms, Confucius on the east wall and a round table at the center.
Chang’s committee today includes connections to Taiwan, Hong Kong, mainland China, Indonesia and the broader diaspora. This year, the Chinese Room committee and the John H. Tsui Memorial Scholarship, named for and seeded by a former chair, together will send seven students to China, Taiwan and Hong Kong.
“We all have different backgrounds,” Chang says. “I just hope this room will bring everybody together.”
On the steps of Florence’s Basilica of Santa Maria Novella, Lina Insana (A&S ’91, ’95G) sits with her students and reads from Giovanni Boccaccio’s “The Decameron,” which opens with 10 young Florentines gathered on those same steps in 1348, fleeing the Black Death.
“It was a wonderful way to read that together in a classroom that wasn’t a classroom at all,” she says. Insana, an associate professor of Italian in the Kenneth P. Dietrich School of Arts and Sciences, has taken students to Italy numerous times. She also knows what a Nationality Rooms scholarship makes possible.

In our latest newsletter, Gro Harlem Brundtland looks ahead to COP31 in Turkey and calls for world leaders to act courageously to tackle climate change.
The climate crisis will not wait for the world’s geopolitics to improve. As leaders gather for COP31 in Turkey next month, half-measures are no longer enough. They must arrive with the courage to act, not just statements to describe the situation. And they must leave Antalya with commitments equal to the scale of the crises we are already experiencing: record heatwaves, devastating floods, and a major energy-security shock created by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The pressures are only mounting. A Super El Niño – exacerbated by climate change - now threatens to increase the risks of drought, extreme heat, floods and storms across the globe. The additional heat alone is projected to cause 450,000 more deaths worldwide. As world leaders prepare for COP31 in Turkey next month, they must have the tenacity and vision to work together to tackle the challenge head on. There must be clear leadership from the COP Presidencies of Australia and Turkey. They must mobilise countries behind a clear and credible plan for tangible progress. As Elders, we are clear on the direction of travel: this is the moment to accelerate the just transition away from fossil fuels and towards clean energy, decisively.
The answer to the twin challenges we face – extreme weather and energy security – cannot be to double down on the energy sources that have left us exposed. Instead, we must accelerate the global transition to secure, affordable and clean energy. France and Germany have set the ball rolling – both publishing national roadmaps with timelines for phasing out the use of coal, oil and gas. We must see more countries following in their footsteps. Throughout my career in public service, I have argued that the way to secure our common future is through solidarity and collective action. These principles are more vital now than ever. Promisingly, we have seen two coalitions emerge over the course of this year: the Santa Marta initiative, focused on accelerating the phase-out of fossil fuels, and Electrify Now, focused on expanding electrification. COP31 offers a key moment to build on this good momentum and for countries, cities and companies to find fresh opportunities for collaboration.
Another area where more progress needs to be made is that of climate finance, which moves far slower than the pace of the climate crisis. It is often those who have contributed the least to global emissions that are now suffering the most. As the world tips over the 1.5 degrees threshold, no community should be left to face a climate disaster without adequate protection.
Those who have had the greatest hand in causing the climate crisis must not shirk their responsibilities. Developed countries must lead in delivering the promised climate finance to help people adapt and respond to climate extremes.
I hope that Turkey and Australia can rally countries at COP31 to respond with greater action and practical partnerships. As extreme weather events and high energy prices are set to continue, the world will be watching.

articles.title_orig: Germany's ex-spy chief arrested for espionage and treason
articles.title_zh: Germany's ex-spy chief arrested for espionage and treason
articles.content_orig:
Police have arrested the former head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence agency , August Hanning, on suspicion of espionage, the federal prosecutor's office announced Tuesday.
Hanning served as the agency's chief from December 1998 to November 2005 before moving to the Federal Interior Ministry, where he worked as state secretary until November 2009.
According to a statement from the prosecutor's office, the 80-year-old faces charges including espionage, disclosure of state secrets, attempted treason and working as a secret service agent.
It did not say which foreign intelligence service he is suspected of working for.
The statement added that another former high-ranking BND employee was also arrested on suspicion of providing hundreds of classified documents to Hanning after his tenure as spy chief ended in exchange for payment.
DW's chief political editor Michaela Küfner, reporting from a government press briefing on the arrest, described the case as Germany's "biggest espionage scandal of the century."
Police arrested Hanning early Tuesday at his home in Nordwalde near the western German city of Münster, according to information from WDR, NDR and the daily Süddeutsche Zeitung.
Hanning's alleged accomplice, who was identified only as Manfred D. in line with Germany's privacy laws, was taken into custody in Bavaria.
Authorities were conducting searches at both suspects' properties, as well as in Berlin, the prosecutor said.
During Hanning's tenure as spy head, D. served as his chief of staff. He also subsequently worked under Hanning at the Interior Ministry until 2009.
He is facing charges of "aiding and abetting attempted treason and espionage against the state."
Marc Henrichmann, who chairs the German parliament's intelligence oversight committee, said following the arrests that Germany "will not tolerate the betrayal of secrets."
"Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out," he said in comments to the AFP news agency.
German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz, also a member of the oversight committee, said the allegations were "deeply troubling" and called for a "swift and thorough investigation."
The investigation into Hanning reportedly began due to his connection to a high-profile trial involving businesswoman Christine Block.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The prosecutor's office said Hanning and Manfred D. are believed to have come up with their arrangement in 2010.
From 2012 to March 2026, D. served as chief of staff to Hanning's successors at the BND spy agency, where he had access to a wealth of classified documents, according to the prosecutor's statement.
"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement said.
It added that D. is alleged to have provided Hanning with information until at least mid-2022, and that Hanning used that information in his private consulting work.
"In one instance, there is suspicion that Mr. Hanning used classified information to prepare an analysis for an employee of a foreign intelligence service," Ines Peterson, a spokesperson for the federal prosecutor's office, told German broadcaster RTL.
The prosecutor's statement said Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D., for several years."
Hanning and D. are expected to appear before an investigating judge on Tuesday and Wednesday.
